questions.q: In CL.TE, how does the front-end decide the request body length?
o: It reads Transfer-Encoding chunk size markers in the body
It trusts Content-Length and forwards that many bytes
It stops at the Connection: keep-alive header and ignores CL
It always forwards a fixed 1 KB slice of the TCP stream
questions.x: The front-end uses Content-Length. In the usual probe that value covers the zero chunk and the extra SMUGGLED bytes, so the front-end forwards all of them to the back-end.
questions.h: CL stands for Content-Length. Which server in CL.TE uses CL, and what does it do with that number?

questions.q: In CL.TE, where does the back-end think the request body ends?
o: At the exact byte count given in the Content-Length header
At the zero-size chunk used by Transfer-Encoding: chunked
When the TCP connection is fully closed by the front-end
After a fixed idle timeout if no more bytes have arrived
questions.x: The back-end uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked and stops at chunk size 0. Bytes after that, such as SMUGGLED, stay in the socket buffer and are treated as the start of the next request.
questions.h: TE stands for Transfer-Encoding. What marker ends a chunked body?

questions.q: What happens to bytes after the zero-size chunk in a CL.TE probe?
o: The front-end drops them because Content-Length already ended
They stay in the back-end buffer and prefix the next request
The back-end returns them to the client as a 100-continue
They are logged and then discarded before the next request
questions.x: The front-end already forwarded those leftover bytes as part of Content-Length. The back-end thought the request ended at the zero chunk, so the extra bytes wait in the buffer and are prepended to whatever arrives next on that connection.
questions.h: The back-end stopped at chunk 0. The extra bytes did not vanish. Where do they sit until another request arrives?

questions.q: How do differential responses confirm CL.TE smuggling?
o: Odd-numbered requests get extra headers that even ones lack
A follow-up GET / comes back 404 instead of the usual 200
A slow first response and a fast second one prove buffering
Two status codes inside one response mean the parser split
questions.x: Timing delays can hint at smuggling. A stronger proof is a different status than a normal request to the same path. If you smuggle GET /404 and the next request to / gets 404 instead of 200, the leftover prefix was applied.
questions.h: You request / and expect 200. After the attack request you get 404 for /. What was prepended onto that second request?

questions.q: After the attack request, how should the confirming request be sent?
o: On the same client TCP connection, to a different host header
On a different client connection, targeting the same URL path
As HTTP/2 only, so the front-end cannot rewrite the body
After waiting one minute so the back-end buffer can expire
questions.x: Send the second request on a different client connection, still to the same URL so load balancing can hit the same back-end. A dummy header such as X-Ignore on the smuggled request absorbs the start of that real request so header parsing does not break before /404 is read.
questions.h: The leftover bytes live on the back-end socket, not on your first client connection. How do you still hit that same back-end?
